newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cairns Group set on more farm trade reform in 1999.
newsitem.headline: Cairns Group set on more farm trade reform in 1999.

text.p: The Cairns Group of agricultural exporting nations will be seeking far-reaching reform of world farm trade in negotiations scheduled for 1999, said a statement after a ministerial meeting in Rio de Janeiro.

At the end of two days of talks, ministers stressed they were determined that the negotiations, set out under the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agriculture Agreement, should both begin on time and be conducted swiftly.

"To this end ministers have instructed officials to undertake as a matter of urgency the necessary analysis and preparation of options and strategies for all the key areas of agriculture requiring reform by the time of the next Cairns Ministerial meeting in 1998," a statement said.

Formed in 1986, the Cairns Group operates under Australian leadership on an informal basis. Its members range from Thailand to Uruguay and account for about 20 percent of the world's agricultural exports.
In order to foster broader support for further agricultural liberalisation, ministers said they were willing to consider applications from possible new members.
The Rio de Janeiro meeting was the first in which Paraguay participated as a full member, bring to 15 the number of Cairns Group countries.
South Africa, which also attended this week's meeting as a observer, has formally requested to join the Group and could be received as a full member at the next meeting, officials said.

In a communique, the ministers also expressed support for new WTO members on terms which were acceptable to all WTO members and in the understanding they would "comply fully with WTO disciplines, particularly those relating to market access, domestic support and export subsidies."
Argentina's Agriculture Secretary Felipe Carlos Sola said today however at a press conference the Group's members are concerned about the possible memberships of China and Russia.
"The countries which are joining up do not offer the right kind of concessions for trade. They want to join at no cost, without improving the market," Sola told reporters.
Sola also criticised the U.S. for not taking the concerns of other countries into account when negotiating over trade, particularly in the case of China.

"The U.S. sorts out its problems and then expects everyone else to receive the new countries with open arms when in fact we lose out," he said. "We don't want countries joining the WTO to be subject to conditions less strict than those for existing members," he added.
